section.title: The Mind of Christ
section.sectionRationale: Here the letter turns to its central exhortation and its theological summit. Paul calls the church to a life worthy of the gospel, standing firm and united even under opposition, then grounds unity in humility that counts others more important than self. To fuel that humility he sets before them the mind of Christ, sung in the great hymn of the Son who emptied Himself to the point of death on a cross and was exalted by God to the name above every name.
section.thesis: Believers are to live worthy of the gospel, standing firm and united without fear of opponents, pursuing a humility that puts others first, and this humility is fueled by the mind of Christ, who though in the form of God emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to death on a cross, for which God exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name, that every knee should bow and every tongue confess Him Lord.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to a gospel-worthy, united, fearless life; the appeal to humility that considers others more important; and the hymn of Christ's self-emptying descent and God's exaltation of Him to the name above every name.

verses.text: Nevertheless, {{politeuomai|conduct yourselves as citizens}} in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then, whether I come and see you or only hear about you in my absence, I will know that you stand firm in one spirit, contending together as one for the faith of the gospel,
without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you. This is a clear sign of their destruction but of your salvation, and it is from God.
For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him,
since you are encountering the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have.
Therefore if you have any encouragement in Christ, if any comfort from His love, if any fellowship with the Spirit, if any affection and compassion,
then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose.
Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride, but in {{tapeinophrosyne|humility}} consider others more important than yourselves.
Each of you should look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others.
Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus:

units.label: The mind of Christ: descent and exaltation
units.note: he emptied himself, God exalted him

verses.text: Who, existing in the {{morphe|form}} of God, did not consider equality with God {{harpagmos|something to be grasped}},
but {{kenoo|emptied Himself}}, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness.
And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross.
Therefore God {{hyperypsoo|exalted Him to the highest place}} and gave Him the name above all names,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth,
and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is {{kyrios|Lord}}, to the glory of God the Father.

politeuomai.gloss: To live as a citizen, to conduct one's public life. The word would ring in a Roman colony proud of its citizenship. Paul tells the Philippians their true citizenship is in the gospel, so they must live as worthy citizens of Christ's kingdom, a theme he returns to in 3:20.

tapeinophrosyne.gloss: Humility, lowliness of mind. In the ancient world this was often a term of contempt, the mindset of a slave; the gospel transforms it into a virtue. It is not thinking poorly of oneself but freely counting others more important, the very mindset displayed by Christ in the verses that follow.

morphe.gloss: Form, the outward expression of an inward and essential nature. To exist in the form of God is to possess the very nature and status of God, not a mere appearance. The same word describes His taking the form of a servant, a real assumption of the servant's nature, not a disguise.

harpagmos.gloss: Something to be seized, grasped, or clung to for advantage. Though equal with God, the Son did not treat that equality as a prize to exploit for Himself; instead He chose the path of self-giving. The word frames the whole hymn as the opposite of grasping ambition.

kenoo.gloss: To empty, to make of no reputation. The Son emptied Himself not by ceasing to be God but by taking the form of a servant, adding humanity and veiling His glory in obedience. This is the word behind the debated term kenosis; Scripture presents it as self-giving addition and lowliness, not subtraction of deity.

hyperypsoo.gloss: To exalt to the highest place, to raise supremely high. In answer to the Son's self-humbling to the depth of the cross, God raised Him to the utmost height and gave Him the name above every name. The word marks the great reversal at the hymn's turning point, the descent answered by exaltation.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master, the word the Greek Old Testament used for the divine name. To confess Jesus Christ as Lord is to give Him the title of God Himself. The universal confession fulfills Isaiah 45, where every knee bows and every tongue swears to the LORD, now directed to Jesus, to the glory of the Father.

basic.context: Paul now gives the church its marching orders: live as citizens worthy of the gospel, stand together, and do not be scared by those who oppose you, for suffering for Christ is itself a gift. Unity like that grows only from humility, so Paul tells them to count others more important than themselves. Then he lifts their eyes to the supreme example, Christ, who though He was God did not cling to His rights but emptied Himself, became a servant, and obeyed all the way to a criminal's cross, so God raised Him high and gave Him the name above every name.
basic.hermeneutics: The exhortation and the hymn belong together. Paul is not merely teaching doctrine about Christ; he is holding up Christ's mind as the pattern for the church's life. The hymn of verses 6 to 11 is the theological engine that drives the practical call to humility and unity.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul tells them to politeuomai, to live as citizens, worthy of the gospel. Unity grows from tapeinophrosyne, humility. The hymn says the Son was in the morphe, the form and nature, of God, yet did not treat equality with God as harpagmos, a thing to grasp; instead He did kenoo, emptied Himself, taking a servant's form. So God did hyperypsoo, supremely exalted Him, that every tongue confess Jesus as kyrios, Lord.
basic.typology: Christ is the true and obedient man where Adam grasped to be like God, the Son let go and obeyed. He is the servant of Isaiah who is exalted after suffering. And the universal confession fulfills Isaiah 45, where God swears that every knee will bow to Him alone, now fulfilled in Jesus.
basic.christ: This hymn is one of the highest views of Christ in Scripture. He is God by nature, yet He humbled Himself to the lowest point, death on a cross, and God exalted Him to the highest place, giving Him the divine name and universal worship. The path down into servanthood and up to the throne is the very shape of the gospel.
basic.god: God the Father is the one who exalts the Son and to whose glory every confession is made. We see a God whose greatness is displayed in self-giving love, who honors the humble, and who is glorified precisely in the exaltation of the crucified Christ as Lord of all.
basic.crossReferences: John 13 shows Jesus washing feet, the mind of the servant. Isaiah 45 promises every knee will bow to God. 2 Corinthians 8:9 says the rich Christ became poor for our sake.
basic.oneStory: Where Adam reached up to seize equality with God and fell, the Son who truly was equal with God stooped down, obeyed, and lifted humanity with Him. The whole story of grasping and falling is reversed by the One who let go and was exalted, and it ends with all creation confessing Him Lord.

context.literary:
This section runs from 1:27 to 2:11 and has the shape of an argument that peaks in a poem. Verses 1:27 to 30 give the call, a single sentence of command with two participles, standing firm and contending together, and two reasons, that the enemy's opposition is a sign and that suffering is a gift. Verses 2:1 to 4 tighten the call into an appeal to the heart: four 'if' clauses that assume the answer yes, a plea to make Paul's joy complete, and a pair of prohibitions and positives about ambition and humility. Verse 5 turns the corner with the demand that the church take on Christ's own mind, and verses 6 to 11 deliver the pattern in a form that reads like a hymn.

The hymn is carefully built. It has two movements of roughly equal weight. In the first, verses 6 to 8, the Son is the subject of every verb and every verb moves downward: existing in the form of God, not grasping, emptying, taking, being made, being found, humbling, becoming obedient. In the second, verses 9 to 11, the subject changes to God and the movement is upward: exalted, gave the name, bow, confess. The turning point is the word 'therefore' at the start of verse 9, and the lowest point is the phrase 'even death on a cross' at the end of verse 8. Many readers hear a V shape: down to the cross, then up to the throne.

The hymn is not a detour. Paul has used the words 'mind' and 'humility' in the lead-in, and the pattern of the Son's choices answers each in turn, as the church is told to 'consider others more important,' and the Son 'did not consider equality with God something to be grasped.' The whole section also fits the letter's larger movement: it follows Paul's own example in 1:12 to 26 and precedes the models of Timothy and Epaphroditus in 2:19 to 30.
context.historical:
Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens took pride in their Roman standing. In such a place the word politeuomai, to live as a citizen, would sound distinctly Roman. A culture built on honour, rank and public standing is exactly the soil in which 'selfish ambition' and 'empty pride' grow, and the instruction to count others more important would have cut against the social grain. Lowliness of mind, tapeinophrosyne, was in the ancient world typically a term of reproach for a slavish attitude, and Paul uses it as a virtue.

The church faced opposition. Acts 16 records the founding events, a public beating and imprisonment of Paul and Silas, and 1 Thessalonians 2:2 says Paul suffered and was shamefully treated at Philippi. The people who now oppose the Philippian believers are probably local officials and neighbours who regard them as disloyal to the civic cult and to the emperor, though the text says only 'those who oppose you.' Paul's statement that the same struggle is theirs and his in 1:30 draws a line from their founding to their present.

The cross was the most shameful death in the empire, reserved for slaves and rebels, and a Roman citizen was normally spared it. For Philippians proud of their citizenship, the phrase 'even death on a cross' would have been a shock. Verses 9 to 11 also take on a public edge. Under the empire, subjects were expected to hail Caesar as lord, and the confession that 'Jesus Christ is Lord' makes a rival claim. Paul does not make it a political slogan; he places it within worship, 'to the glory of God the Father.'
context.canonical:
The hymn is rich in Scripture. Its closing lines quote Isaiah 45:22 and 23, where the LORD declares that He is God and there is no other, and swears that every knee will bow before Him and every tongue swear allegiance. Paul applies this oath to Jesus, and Romans 14:11 quotes it of every knee bowing to God at His judgment seat, so Paul treats the oath as God's own claim, and then in Philippians places Jesus within it. The 'name above all names' is the name of the LORD, Isaiah 42:8, which He will not give to another.

The pattern of descent and exaltation draws on the Servant of Isaiah, who 'will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted,' Isaiah 52:13, after being 'numbered with the transgressors' and 'poured out' to death, Isaiah 53:12. The word 'servant' in 2:7 is doulos, a slave, and Isaiah's Hebrew word for his Servant, ebed, belongs to the same field of meaning, so the pattern of suffering followed by glory matches. Many also hear Adam behind the hymn. In Genesis 3:5 the serpent promised that the pair would be like God, and Adam grasped at it. The Son, truly in God's form, refuses to treat His rank as a thing to exploit.

The New Testament repeats the movement in its own ways. John 1:1 and 14, the Word who was God and became flesh, Colossians 1:15 to 20 and 2:9, Hebrews 1:3 and 2:9, and 1 Timothy 3:16 all tell of the One who was in the glory and came down and was lifted up. Revelation 5:12 and 13 gives the final scene, where every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth joins in praise to the Lamb who was slain, so that Paul's three-level universe in verse 10 comes true.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant the hymn to do work in a church that was threatened by division. He did not quote it merely to show how high his view of Christ was, though it does that. He meant it as an argument from Christ's character to the church's conduct: since Christ chose the path of giving up and serving, no member of His church has any right to treat rank or reputation as a thing to be held. The church's quarrel is therefore not just a social problem; it is a failure to share the mind of the Lord they confess.

He also meant to comfort. The same hymn that calls for humility says that God vindicates those who walk it, 'Therefore God exalted Him.' The Philippians, facing opposition and ridicule, could read the hymn as a promise that the way of the cross ends at God's throne. The contrast with the surrounding culture, where the powerful were honoured and the weak were despised, is deliberate. Paul wanted them to see that their place in the world, which looked low, was actually the place where Christ had gone first. Their suffering, he says in 1:29, is a gift, and their unity in humility is the visible mark of their salvation, as 1:28 hints.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The section combines commands with a great description. The commands are firm: live as citizens worthy of the gospel, stand firm, do nothing from selfish ambition, count others more important, look to others' interests, take on the mind of Christ. The hymn itself is description, a record of what the Son did and what God did in answer. It is not given as a template for believers to copy in every detail, since no believer can empty himself of divine form or earn a name above all names. What is prescriptive is the attitude: the Son's readiness to give up His own advantages for the sake of others.

Two cautions help the church apply it. First, the humility commanded here is not a low estimate of one's gifts or an invitation to be walked over; Paul himself speaks with authority and urges the Philippians to be bold. It is a willingness to use whatever one has for others. Second, the exaltation in verses 9 to 11 is God's act, not a reward the church may seek by being humble. The church imitates Christ's self-giving, not His seeking of the name; the sequence in the text is obedience first and honour from God afterwards, and that honour belongs to Christ alone.

debates.question: What does harpagmos mean in verse 6, and does the hymn presuppose that the Son was already divine?

views.label: Something already held that He did not exploit
views.case: The phrase 'existing in the form of God' uses a present participle, and 'equality with God' is something He already had. On this reading, a thing grasped (res retinenda, in the old Latin tag) means a prize to be held onto or exploited, and the Son chose not to do this, which makes sense only if He already had it. Most patristic writers and many modern commentators read it this way, and the text is taken as a strong witness to pre-existence.

views.label: Something not yet possessed that He refused to seize
views.case: Others say harpagmos means something snatched, a prize to be seized that was not yet in hand, in contrast with Adam, who reached for it. The Son does not seize, and God gives. In this reading the hymn is built on an Adam-Christ contrast, and it can still be consistent with His deity if the refusal is understood as His own choice.

debates.bearing: Both views take the hymn as a statement about Christ's character and Paul's call to humility, and most scholars who hold either also hold that the Son is divine and pre-existent. The disagreement is over the word's nuance, not over whether the Son was God. The application is the same: the one who had every claim to glory did not use it for Himself.

debates.question: What does it mean that Christ emptied Himself (kenosis)?

views.label: Self-giving addition, not loss of deity
views.case: He emptied Himself by taking the form of a servant and being made in human likeness; the emptying is His humbling and adding of humanity, veiling His glory in obedience, not surrendering His divine nature.

views.label: Laying aside divine attributes
views.case: Some kenotic theories argue the Son gave up certain divine attributes in the incarnation; this strains the text and endangers His full deity, which the hymn everywhere assumes.

debates.bearing: The orthodox reading keeps Christ fully God even in the manger and on the cross; the emptying is the greatness of His condescension, not a diminishing of His deity.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's opening verb, politeuomai, takes its root from polis, city, and in verse 27 it is a command to behave as citizens, a verb used elsewhere in the New Testament only at Acts 23:1. The same ring returns with the noun politeuma at 3:20, where their citizenship is in heaven. The sense in 1:27 is conduct that fits the gospel's own constitution.

The next two participles are sports terms. 'Contending together' is synathlountes, from athleo, to compete as a team of athletes, a picture also at 4:3. 'Standing firm' is stekete, a stance of holding a position. Together they depict a team of fighters holding a line. In verse 29 'it has been granted' is echaristhe, from charis, grace. The same verb comes back in verse 9 of chapter 2, where God 'gave' the name, echarisato. The suffering of believers and the name of the Son are both given as free gifts, a connection that is easy to miss in English.

In 2:1 to 4 the words are warm. 'Fellowship with the Spirit' is koinonia pneumatos, which can mean a shared participation in the Spirit or the Spirit's creating of fellowship among them. 'Like-minded' is a form of phroneo, a verb of mind-set that Paul uses ten times in this letter, in 2:2, 2:5 and 4:2 among others; the Philippians are to share one way of thinking, one disposition. 'Selfish ambition' is eritheia, used at 1:17, and 'empty pride' is kenodoxia, literally empty glory, which shares the root kenos with the verb of verse 7, ekenosen. The pun is that vainglory is empty already, while the Son empties Himself in service. 'More important' translates hyperechontas, literally holding above, a compound whose prefix means over.

In the hymn, 'in the likeness of men' translates homoioma, a word Paul uses at Romans 8:3 of the Son sent 'in the likeness of sinful man,' and 'appearance,' schema, in verse 8 speaks of what is outwardly visible. Verses 7 and 8 stack these terms to say that He truly became a man and was recognised as one, while not ceasing to be what He was. The word 'obedient' is hypekoos, and the phrase 'even death on a cross' stands as a climax added after 'death.' In verse 9 the compound hyperypsoo has a prefix meaning 'above,' and the 'name above every name' matches it in sound. In verse 10, the three realms are epouranion, epigeion and katachthonion, the heavenly, the earthly and the subterranean, a way of naming the whole creation. And in verse 11 'confess' is exomologeo, the verb that the Septuagint uses at Isaiah 45:23, so Paul is quoting Isaiah's oath almost directly.

typology.fulfillment: Adam was made in God's image and listened to the promise that he would be like God, so he reached for it and fell, bringing death. The hymn describes the Son in God's form who does not treat equality as something to seize but empties Himself and obeys to death. The correspondence is a contrast of two men, as Paul draws it elsewhere in Romans 5:19: through one man's disobedience many were made sinners, through one man's obedience many will be made righteous. The escalation is that where Adam brought exile, the Son brings the exaltation that believers will share, Philippians 3:21. The type falls short because Adam's attempt was a reach upward, while the Son's act was a descent from a height Adam never held.

Isaiah's Servant is exalted, lifted up and highly exalted, after bearing the sin of many and being numbered with the transgressors. Philippians 2:7 to 9 follows the same movement of humiliation and elevation, using the word 'servant' for the form He took and the verb of exaltation for the answer. The correspondence is both of the pattern and of the vindication by God. The escalation is that the Servant is also the Lord, so the exalted one receives the name of the LORD. The type falls short in that Isaiah did not name the Servant's divinity, which the hymn makes plain.

The LORD swears by Himself that every knee will bow and every tongue swear allegiance to Him alone, and the context says there is no other God. In verses 10 and 11 the same oath is fulfilled in Jesus, to whom every knee bows and every tongue confesses that He is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. The correspondence is word for word. The escalation is that Jesus is placed within the identity of the one God, since the glory of the Father is not rivalled but served by the Son's exaltation. The pattern falls short in the sense that the oath is still being fulfilled, since the bowing is finished only on the last day, Romans 14:10 and 11.

study.christ:
This passage is one of the greatest statements about Christ in the New Testament, and the way it is built shows how Paul thinks of Him. The hymn begins with His eternal identity and ends with His universal rule, and it does not stop to prove either. The first claim is that He existed in the form of God. The word 'form' points to the real nature behind outward appearance, and 'equality with God' is something He possessed. John 1:1, John 5:18 and Colossians 2:9 say the same in different words. The hymn therefore does not describe a man promoted to godhood but God the Son who chose to serve.

The second claim concerns what He did with that status. He did not treat it as something to take advantage of, and the next lines say what He did instead. To empty Himself is defined by what follows, not by what is lost: 'taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness.' He did not stop being God; He added what He was not, and He did it in the lowest way, the path of obedience that ended in a slave's execution. The cross was, under Deuteronomy 21:23 and Galatians 3:13, a place of curse, and the hymn says He went there willingly, as John 10:17 and 18 shows, laying down His life of His own accord.

The third claim is the Father's answer. Verse 9 begins 'Therefore,' and the word suggests that the exaltation is the Father's vindication of the Son's path. The phrase 'the name above all names' is the name of the LORD, Isaiah 42:8, which means that Jesus is called by the very name that Israel reserved for God. Acts 2:36 puts it as God making Jesus both Lord and Christ, and Romans 10:9 makes confession of His lordship the heart of the gospel.

There is one more link. Hebrews 5:8 says that although He was a Son He learned obedience from what He suffered, and 2 Corinthians 8:9 says that though He was rich He became poor so that we might become rich. Both say the same as the hymn, that the gospel is not first an example but a rescue. Paul uses Christ as a pattern for the church's mind in verse 5, but the hymn describes what no believer could do, and what Christ did for them. The pattern depends on the work.
study.god:
The passage gives one of the Bible's clearest pictures of a God whose greatness is shown in giving, not grasping. The Son, who is 'in the form of God,' reveals what that form is by what He does with it: He serves. The God of the Bible is not a being who guards rank. He is generous to the point of the cross, and the cross, far from contradicting His glory, displays it. John 1:14 says the glory of the Word made flesh was full of grace and truth, and Philippians 2 says the same thing in other terms.

It also shows God as Father and Son together, in distinct roles within one honour. The Son empties Himself and the Father exalts Him; the Son receives the name and the Father is glorified by every confession. Nothing in the hymn lets the exaltation of the Son become a rival to the Father. Every knee bows to Jesus, and the result is 'to the glory of God the Father.' This is why the church has always taught the deity of the Son and the oneness of God together: Isaiah 45 says the LORD shares His glory with no other, Philippians says the glory goes to the Father through the Son, and 1 Corinthians 8:6 says there is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ.

God is the one who exalts the humble. The movement from 'humbled Himself' to 'God exalted Him' is the pattern of God's government throughout Scripture, as in 1 Samuel 2:7 and 8 and Luke 14:11. The God who acts here is therefore not arbitrary; He honours a particular kind of life. That is a comfort to a persecuted church and a challenge to an ambitious one.

God is sovereign over suffering. In 1:29 He grants it as well as faith, and in 2:13, just after the hymn, He is the one who works in believers to will and to act. The word 'granted' means that opposition does not catch Him by surprise. A church that fears its opponents is reminded that the same God who exalted the crucified Lord has given it a share in His path.

For worship, the passage supplies one of the earliest Christian hymns and invites the church to sing it as its own. It teaches that to worship Jesus is not to compete with God but to honour Him, and that the right response to divine humility is not pride but awe.

crossReferences.note: The LORD swears by Himself that every knee will bow and every tongue swear allegiance, and says there is no other God. Philippians 2:10 and 11 apply this oath to Jesus, which shows that Paul sees the Lord Jesus as the one in whom the one God receives the world's worship.

The Servant 'will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted.' The movement from servant to exaltation is the Old Testament pattern behind the second half of the hymn, and the verb of exaltation in Philippians 2:9 echoes it.

The serpent promises, 'you will be like God.' Set beside Philippians 2:6, it frames the hymn as a reversal of Adam's grasping, so that the one who truly was in God's form refuses to exploit it, while the one who was not reached for it.

Through one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, and through one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. It supplies the doctrine that lies under the hymn, and shows that the obedience 'to death' in Philippians 2:8 is a representative act with consequences for others.

Knowing that the Father had put all things in His hands, Jesus lays aside His garments and washes the disciples' feet. The footwashing is the same pattern lived on a small scale: a person who knows his rank takes the lowest task, and the scene that follows invites the church to do likewise.

Though He was rich, He became poor so that we might become rich. It gives the same descent in financial terms and shows Paul using Christ's self-giving as the standard for how believers give to and care for others, as in Philippians 2:4.

The Son is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn over all creation, all things were created in Him, and through the blood of His cross all things are reconciled. It is a companion hymn that makes explicit the greatness behind Philippians 2:6 and the reach of the cross behind 2:8.

Jesus was made a little lower than the angels and is now crowned with glory and honour because He suffered death. The 'because' mirrors Philippians 2:9's 'therefore,' and the two passages together show that the exaltation follows the death by God's design.

The Lamb who was slain is worthy to receive power, honour and glory, and every creature in heaven, on earth and under the earth joins in praise to the one on the throne and to the Lamb. It shows Philippians 2:10 and 11 fulfilled in the vision of the end.

Christ suffered and left an example to follow in His footsteps, then bore our sins in His body on the tree. Like Philippians 2, it joins the pattern for the church with the work that only He could do, and it warns against reading the hymn as example alone.

study.oneStory:
The hymn tells in a few lines the story that the whole Bible takes up. It begins before creation, with the Son in the form of God, and it ends at the end of history, with every knee bowing. Between the two comes a descent and an ascent that retell and correct the story of Adam. In Genesis 1 and 2 a man is made in God's image and given a place in the garden, and in Genesis 3 he reaches for more than he was given and loses what he had. The Bible's story from there is of God's patient work to bring a new man, who will do what Adam did not do. Paul says that man has come.

The hymn also explains what the story has been about. The Old Testament shows God's people repeatedly failing to give up their own rights and trust God, and the prophets promise a Servant who will bear the sin of many. In Philippians 2 that Servant is also the Lord, and the wonder is that the Lord is the Servant. The gospel is thus not an improvement on Israel's story but its answer: the God who made all things and who was worshipped on the mountain has come down to the cross and has been lifted to the throne.

The passage looks forward as well. The movement from 'granted to suffer' to 'every knee shall bow' sets the church's life inside the same pattern. Believers follow the humiliated Lord now and will share His glory later, as Paul says at 3:10 and 21, and Romans 8:17 says that those who suffer with Him will be glorified with Him. The church's unity in humility is a visible sign in a divided world of what God will do when He brings all things together under Christ, Ephesians 1:10.

The end of the story is in verse 11. Revelation 5 and 7 show the multitude from every nation, and the new creation is a world in which the Lord is acknowledged by every tongue, so that the confusion of Babel is reversed, Genesis 11:1 to 9. In that world no one will grasp, because everyone will have received everything. The glory of God the Father, with which the hymn ends, is the glory that fills the new heaven and earth, Revelation 21:23, and it is the glory that the Son, in His humility, has made possible.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by conducting yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel?

options.text: Living as citizens of Christ's kingdom, standing firm and united for the faith.
options.note: Verse 27 uses citizenship language, calling for a united, gospel-shaped public life.

options.text: Earning the gospel by impressive moral effort.
options.note: The gospel is received by faith; worthy conduct is its fruit, not its price.

options.text: Keeping quiet so opponents leave you alone.
options.note: Paul calls them to contend for the faith without fear, not to hide.

options.text: Living however feels right to each person.
options.note: He calls for a life shaped by and worthy of the gospel of Christ.

quiz.q: According to verses 3 and 4, what is the root of Christian unity?

options.text: Humility that counts others more important and looks to their interests.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 ground unity in humility, not selfish ambition.

options.text: Everyone insisting on their own rights.
options.note: That is selfish ambition, the opposite of what Paul commands.

options.text: Ignoring differences and never speaking honestly.
options.note: Unity comes from humble love, not from mere avoidance.

options.text: Competition to prove who is most important.
options.note: Paul forbids empty pride and selfish ambition.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Christ emptied Himself?

options.text: He took the form of a servant and became human, veiling His glory in obedience.
options.note: Verse 7 defines the emptying as taking a servant's form, not losing deity.

options.text: He gave up being God during His time on earth.
options.note: A common kenotic error; the hymn assumes His full deity throughout.

options.text: He only appeared to be human but was not.
options.note: He was made in human likeness and found in appearance as a man, truly human.

options.text: He stopped existing for a time.
options.note: The Son never ceased to be; He humbled Himself by adding humanity.

quiz.q: Why did God exalt Jesus to the highest place?

options.text: Because He humbled Himself and became obedient to death on a cross.
options.note: The Therefore of verse 9 links exaltation to His self-humbling obedience.

options.text: Because Jesus demanded to be honored.
options.note: He did not grasp; the exaltation is God's answer to His humility.

options.text: Because the crowds forced God's hand.
options.note: The exaltation is God's own free act in response to Christ's obedience.

options.text: For no particular reason.
options.note: Paul gives a clear reason, His obedience unto death.

quiz.q: What is the final goal of every knee bowing and tongue confessing Jesus as Lord?

options.text: The glory of God the Father.
options.note: Verse 11 ends with to the glory of God the Father.

options.text: The exaltation of the church.
options.note: The church shares in Christ's glory, but the stated goal is the Father's glory.

options.text: The pride of individual believers.
options.note: The hymn is about Christ's honor and the Father's glory, not human pride.

options.text: Nothing beyond the confession itself.
options.note: Paul names the goal, the glory of God the Father.

questions: Paul says even suffering for Christ is a gift granted to you. How does calling suffering a gift, rather than only a hardship, change the way you face opposition?
Humility means counting others more important than yourself. Where is God asking you to look to someone else's interests this week rather than your own?
Christ did not cling to His rights but let them go for our sake. What right or advantage are you tempted to grasp that Christ might be calling you to release?
The path of Christ went down into servanthood before God lifted Him up. Where are you seeking to rise that God may be calling you first to stoop?
One day every knee will bow to Jesus as Lord. How does living now in light of that certain future reshape your priorities today?

translationNotes.note: Something to be grasped renders harpagmos; the BSB footnote notes the alternative something to be exploited. Either way the Son did not use equality with God for His own advantage.
Emptied Himself translates ekenosen, the source of the term kenosis; the following words define it as taking a servant's form, not surrendering deity.
